subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Venus: Earth's Evil Twin
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Venus: Earth's Evil Twin.

hook.text: Venus is nearly the same size as Earth. But its surface temperature melts lead—at 465°C.

buildup.text: A thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect. Surface pressure is 90 times Earth's.

discovery.text: Soviet Venera probes landed on Venus in the 1970s. They lasted minutes before being crushed and melted.

twist.text: Venus rotates backward and so slowly that one day is longer than one year. Nobody knows why it flipped.

climax.text: Phosphine gas was detected in Venus's clouds in 2020—a possible hint of life. The debate rages on.

punchline.text: Earth's twin chose a different path. A greenhouse gone wrong.

quiz.question: What happened to the Soviet Venera probes that landed on Venus?
options: They were crushed and melted within minutes by extreme heat and pressure
They orbited Venus for years collecting data
They bounced off the thick atmosphere and returned to space

details.summary: Venus is nearly Earth's twin in size and mass but has a runaway greenhouse atmosphere of 96% carbon dioxide, surface temperatures of 465°C (hotter than Mercury), and crushing surface pressure 90 times Earth's. Thick sulfuric acid clouds hide the surface completely.
details.whyItMatters: Venus is a warning about runaway greenhouse effects — it may once have had oceans and a habitable climate. Understanding how Venus became a hellscape reveals what could happen to Earth under extreme climate change and informs the search for…
takeaways: Venus has surface temperatures of 465°C from runaway greenhouse heating
Its atmosphere is 96% CO₂ with sulfuric acid clouds
It rotates backward so slowly its day is longer than its year

faq.question: Could Venus have once been habitable?
faq.answer: Possibly. Climate models suggest Venus may have had liquid water oceans for up to 2 billion years before a runaway greenhouse effect boiled them away. NASA's VERITAS and DAVINCI+ missions and ESA's EnVision aim to test this hypothesis by studying Venus's surface and atmosphere in detail.

faq.question: What about the phosphine detection controversy?
faq.answer: In 2020, researchers reported detecting phosphine gas in Venus's clouds — a potential biosignature since no known geological process easily produces it there. The detection was quickly challenged by other scientists questioning the data analysis.
